summary: Norwalk packs over 100,000 people into fewer than ten square miles, making it one of the denser cities in southeast Los Angeles County — yet it reads visually as a low-slung residential grid rather than anything approaching urban, because almost nothing rises above two stories. The terrain is dead flat, part of the broad coastal plain between the San Gabriel Mountains and the Pacific, which means open skies and reliably mild weather: annual daytime highs averaging 76°F with roughly 9.4 hours of sunshine per day, so overcast gloom is genuinely rare. Norwalk functions largely as a bedroom community — the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder and Metropolitan State Hospital are among its notable employers, but most working residents commute outward, with the I-5 and I-605 freeways forming the city's eastern and western spines. A median home price around $617,000 against a median household income near $99,000 yields a price-to-income ratio just above 6:1, which is steep but notably below many neighboring L.A. County cities; rents averaging about $2,000 keep the gap between owning and renting tangible. The Norwalk/Santa Fe Springs Metrolink station connects to downtown L.A., offering an alternative to freeway gridlock. Motor vehicle theft runs high at 577 per 100,000, a number worth weighing. Norwalk is the kind of place where affordability relative to its surroundings is the main draw — and that relative advantage is also the clearest signal of its limitations.
